stages.title: A UK customer signs up at example.co.uk
stages.summary: The record is created when the customer submits the form. The .uk domain is registered with the UK registry, Nominet, so the name itself sits under UK law.

stages.title: The record crosses international networks
stages.summary: Seconds later the record leaves the UK for servers in India. On the way it passes through networks where three countries have interception powers.

stages.title: Stored in an Indian data centre
stages.summary: The record is written to disk in India. Where the data physically sits brings in Indian law, whoever owns the company.

stages.title: Run by the US operator
stages.summary: Every day after, a US company administers the record remotely. US law follows the company, not the server, so the record is within US reach without leaving India.

stages.title: An agency asks for the record
stages.summary: Months later an authority wants the record. Agreements between countries, and conflicts between their laws, decide who can get it and how.

powers.name: Domain suspension
powers.allows: Nominet can suspend .uk domains at the request of UK law enforcement.
powers.here: This can take the service offline at the moment of sign-up, without touching the data. It affects availability rather than access, so it sits outside the core score.

powers.name: Investigatory Powers Act 2016
powers.allows: Interception, equipment interference and bulk powers, with warrants approved by a Judicial Commissioner. Technical capability notices can require providers to maintain access capabilities. Amended in 2024.
powers.here: Bulk interception warrants can cover communications leaving the UK, so the record can be collected before it reaches India.

powers.name: Executive Order 12333
powers.allows: Authorises NSA signals intelligence collection outside the US, with oversight largely within the executive branch.
powers.here: The US can collect the record on international networks outside the US, before the US company ever touches it.

powers.name: Five Eyes intelligence sharing
powers.allows: Under the UKUSA arrangements GCHQ and the NSA share signals intelligence, so data collected by one can reach the other.
powers.here: Whatever either country collects in transit can end up with the other, so the record is exposed to both through a single interception.

powers.name: Telecommunications Act 2023
powers.allows: Section 20 and the 2024 interception rules let the Union Home Secretary order interception of messages, reviewed by a committee of senior officials.
powers.here: Once the record enters Indian networks it can be intercepted on Indian orders, with review inside the executive rather than by a court.

sources.label: Department of Telecommunications: Acts and rules

powers.name: IT Act 2000, section 69
powers.allows: Lets the government direct interception, monitoring or decryption of information by authorised agencies such as the Intelligence Bureau. Intermediaries must assist.
powers.here: The stored record can be monitored or decrypted on government direction, and the hosting provider must help.

powers.name: DPDP Act 2023
powers.allows: Rules notified in November 2025 phase in until May 2027. The government can exempt its own agencies on security grounds and require organisations to provide information.
powers.here: The data protection law that should protect the record also lets the government exempt itself and call for information.

powers.name: RBI payment-data rule
powers.allows: The Reserve Bank of India requires payment system data to be stored only in India.
powers.here: If the record includes payment data it must stay in India, which keeps it within Indian powers and limits where it can be moved.

sources.label: RBI: Storage of payment system data

powers.name: CLOUD Act
powers.allows: Allows the DOJ and FBI to compel US companies to provide data regardless of where it is stored.
powers.here: Because the operator is a US company, a US order can require it to produce the record held in India.

sources.label: CLOUD Act (H.R. 4943, in the Consolidated Appropriations Act 2018)

powers.name: FISA Section 702
powers.allows: Targeting of non-US persons abroad with compelled help from US providers. The statutory authority lapsed in June 2026, but collection continues under court certifications approved in March 2026.
powers.here: The UK customer is a non-US person, so the US operator can be compelled to help collect their record.

sources.label: Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act 2024

powers.name: National Security Letters
powers.allows: Lets the FBI issue secret demands for certain records, with gag orders that limit transparency.
powers.here: The operator can be ordered to hand over records about the account and be barred from telling the customer.

powers.name: UK-US Data Access Agreement
powers.allows: In force since October 2022 under the CLOUD Act. Each country's authorities can serve orders for serious-crime investigations directly on the other's providers.
powers.here: A UK agency can serve its order directly on the US operator, without going through the US government.

sources.label: UK-USA Agreement on Access to Electronic Data

powers.name: Corporate control
powers.allows: US authorities can compel a US parent company to produce data held by its Indian operations.
powers.here: Keeping the record in India does not keep it out of US reach: the demand goes to the parent company, which controls the Indian servers.

powers.name: Conflict of laws
powers.allows: A US order to produce data held in India may conflict with Indian law, leaving the provider unable to comply with both.
powers.here: The operator may face penalties whichever way it decides, and the customer has little say in the outcome.
